title: Genesis 23. The Cup Buried.
edition: AID Genesis, Layer 1 (the steward's manuscript); narration: Kristin voice (public domain)
level_note: text follows the narration phrase by phrase
verse_numbers: none in this text; none shown
phrases: Genesis 23. The Cup Buried.
Sarah lived one hundred and twenty-seven years.
These were the years of Sarah's life.
The only woman in Scripture whose age at death is recorded.
Not Eve.
Not Rebekah.
Not Rachel.
Not Deborah.
Not Mary.
Sarah.
The woman who was barren,
who was renamed for a mother of nations,
who laughed behind a tent flap and lied about it,
who was taken by Pharaoh and taken by Abimelech,
who gave her servant to her husband and then demanded the servant's exile,
who held Isaac at the set time and said:
God has made laughter for me.
This woman, whose years are counted and named, dies.
Sarah died in Kiriath-arba, that is, Hebron, in the land of Canaan.
And Abraham came to mourn for Sarah and to weep for her.
Abraham weeps.
The man who did not weep when he was told to offer Isaac.
The man who rose early in the morning and saddled his donkey without a word.
That man weeps now.
The Cup that was carried through flood and covenant and testing has arrived at a tent where the woman who held it is gone.
Sarah, who was with Abraham from Ur, through Haran, through Canaan,
through Egypt, through Gerar, through Beersheba, through Moriah, is dead.
And Abraham weeps.
Then he stands up.
He stands up from before his dead and speaks to the children of Heth:
I am a stranger and a sojourner among you.
Give me a possession of a burial place among you,
that I may bury my dead out of my sight.
The man who was promised all the land of Canaan,
from the river of Egypt to the Euphrates,
ten nations named in a deed sealed by God's oath,
now describes himself as a stranger.
A sojourner.
The Cup that includes nations and kings and stars and dust is held by a man who does not own enough ground to bury his wife.
The promise that was sworn by God Himself has not yet produced a single acre Abraham can call his own.
The children of Heth answer: Hear us, my lord.
You are a prince of God among us.
Bury your dead in the choicest of our tombs.
None of us will withhold his tomb from you.
Bury your dead.
A prince of God.
The Hittites recognize what the promise said before Abraham saw it.
The man who calls himself a stranger is called a prince by the people of the land.
They offer him any tomb for free.
The choicest.
The best.
The Cup that was carried by a sojourner is acknowledged by the residents.
But Abraham refuses.
He rises.
He bows.
He insists:
If you agree that I should bury my dead out of my sight,
hear me and intercede for me with Ephron the son of Zohar,
that he may sell me the cave of Machpelah, which he owns,
which is at the end of his field.
For the full price,
let him sell it to me among you as a possession for a burial place.
Abraham will not take the land as a gift.
He will buy it.
The man who refused Sodom's wealth, not a thread,
not a sandal strap, now refuses the Hittites' generosity.
The same principle: the Cup is filled by God,
or it is not filled at all.
The land that God promised cannot be received as a favor from men.
It must be owned.
Purchased.
Legally transferred in the presence of witnesses.
The man who holds the promise by faith now holds it by deed.
Ephron the Hittite was sitting among the children of Heth.
He answers in the hearing of all who went in at the gate of his city:
No, my lord, hear me.
I give you the field.
And I give you the cave that is in it.
In the presence of the children of my people I give it to you.
Bury your dead.
Ephron offers the field for free.
The same offer the children of Heth made.
The same generosity.
The same refusal to take payment.
But Abraham insists.
He speaks to Ephron in the hearing of the people of the land:
If you will, please hear me.
I will give the price of the field.
Take it from me, and I will bury my dead there.
Ephron answers: My lord, listen to me.
A piece of land worth four hundred shekels of silver,
what is that between you and me?
Bury your dead.
The price is named in the same breath as the offer to give it freely.
Ephron says: it is worth four hundred shekels,
but what is that between us?
The negotiation is performed in the ancient form,
the seller names a price while offering it as a gift,
and the buyer insists on paying.
But Abraham does not counter.
He does not bargain down.
The man who bargained with God from fifty to ten does not bargain with Ephron.
Abraham listened to Ephron.
Abraham weighed out for Ephron the silver he had named in the hearing of the children of Heth,
four hundred shekels of silver, according to the current merchants' standard.
Four hundred shekels.
Paid in full.
Weighed in the presence of witnesses.
The first real estate transaction in Scripture.
The first piece of the promised land that Abraham owns is not a city,
not a field of crops, not a mountain with a view.
It is a grave.
So the field of Ephron, which was in Machpelah,
which was before Mamre, the field, the cave that was in it,
and all the trees that were in the field,
that were in all its borders,
were deeded to Abraham for a possession in the presence of the children of Heth,
before all who went in at the gate of his city.
The deed is complete.
Field.
Cave.
Trees.
Borders.
Witnesses.
The legal language is exact, this is not a metaphor.
This is a title transfer.
The man who was promised the land by God now holds one piece of it by purchase.
The smallest piece.
A burial plot.
But it is his.
Paid for in silver.
Witnessed by the gate.
After this,
Abraham buried Sarah his wife in the cave of the field of Machpelah before Mamre,
that is, Hebron, in the land of Canaan.
The Cup is buried.
Sarah, who carried the promise in her body,
who was the vessel through whom the covenant would come,
who was renamed for a mother of nations,
is laid in the ground of the land she was promised but never owned.
The first acre of the promise is a grave.
The first permanent footprint of the covenant in Canaan is a burial plot purchased from the Hittites with silver weighed at the gate.
The field and the cave were deeded to Abraham by the children of Heth as a possession for a burial place.
The pattern is set.
The promise enters the land through death.
Not through conquest.
Not through a tower.
Not through a city or an army or a name made great.
Through a grave.
The Cup that was held by a woman who is now gone is placed in the ground of the land that was promised to her children.
The covenant that was cut in blood, sealed in flesh,
tested on a mountain, sworn by an oath, now touches the earth.
The first root the promise puts down is in a cave where a woman is buried.
Abraham walks away from the cave.
He has the deed.
He has the field.
He has the trees and the borders and the witnesses.
He does not have Sarah.
The Cup that was carried together is now carried by one.
The man who walked up Moriah with Isaac now walks away from Machpelah alone.
The promise has not changed.
The land is still sworn.
The offspring is still coming.
The nations will still be blessed.
But the vessel that first held the promise in her womb is now held by the ground.
And the ground, for the first time, belongs to Abraham.
The land begins to be claimed through burial.
The Cup is planted.
What grows from it has not yet been seen.
But the seed is in the ground.
